lesson.title: The Cause You Change and the Effect You Measure
lesson.summary: This section defines independent and dependent variables, distinguishes them from variables held constant, and applies the distinction to a classic photosynthesis experiment.
lesson.body:
Every controlled experiment revolves around two key quantities, and biology students need to be able to name both correctly. The independent variable is the factor the experimenter deliberately changes or manipulates. The dependent variable is the outcome that is measured, and it is called "dependent" because its value is expected to depend on, or respond to, changes in the independent variable. Everything else that could plausibly affect the outcome is a controlled variable, something the experimenter deliberately holds constant across all groups so that it cannot explain away the result, which is the practical machinery behind the control groups introduced in the previous section.

A classic experiment used to teach this distinction involves measuring the rate of photosynthesis in an aquatic plant such as Elodea. A sprig of Elodea is submerged in water inside a test tube and placed near a light source. As the plant photosynthesizes, it releases oxygen gas, which can be seen and counted as small bubbles escaping from the cut stem. To test how light intensity affects photosynthesis, a researcher places the light source at several different distances from the plant, since light intensity decreases predictably as distance increases. Distance from the light source, which the researcher directly sets, is the independent variable. The number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute, which the researcher counts but does not directly control, is the dependent variable. Water temperature, the concentration of dissolved carbon dioxide, the species and size of the plant sample, and the duration of each trial are all controlled variables, held as close to identical as possible across every distance tested, so that any change in bubble rate can be attributed to light intensity rather than to some other difference between trials.

This vocabulary matters beyond the classroom because it is exactly how experimental results get communicated and graphed. By convention, the independent variable is plotted on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable on the vertical axis, so a graph of the Elodea experiment would show light intensity along the bottom and bubbles per minute along the side, letting a reader see at a glance that photosynthetic rate rises with light intensity up to a point, then levels off as some other factor, often the carbon dioxide supply, becomes limiting instead.

It is easy to confuse controlled variables with the independent variable, especially when an experiment tests more than one factor. If a researcher wanted to know whether both light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affect photosynthetic rate, the cleanest approach is to test one independent variable at a time, holding the other constant, rather than changing both simultaneously, because changing two things at once makes it impossible to know which change caused any observed effect. This need to isolate one variable at a time is precisely why controlled experiments are structured the way they are, and it is why the hypothesis that motivates the experiment, discussed in the earlier sections of this chapter, should be written specifically enough to name both the independent variable being manipulated and the dependent variable expected to change in response.
